Introduction

The debate over child sexual abuse material (CSAM) is one of the most morally fraught issues of our time. For decades, governments and law enforcement agencies have treated all forms of CSAM—whether depicting real children or AI-generated simulations—as equally abhorrent, criminalizing their creation, distribution, and possession without distinction. The Problem: Criminalizing AI CSAM Perpetuates Real Exploitation

1. The Illusion of Moral Equivalence

Proponents of the current legal framework argue that AI-generated CSAM is "just as harmful" as real CSAM because it normalizes and glorifies child sexual abuse. While this claim is emotionally compelling, it is factually and logically flawed. Real CSAM is a crime of commission—it documents and perpetuates the sexual violence against a real child. AI-generated CSAM, by contrast, is a crime of simulation—it involves no victim, no trauma, and no physical harm.

To equate the two is like comparing a snuff film (real murder) to a horror movie (fictional violence). One is a documentation of a real crime; the other is a fictional representation. Criminalizing both treats the symptom (AI CSAM) as severely as the disease (real CSAM), while doing nothing to address the root cause.

2. The Underground Market Thrives on Prohibition

History has shown that prohibiting harmful content does not eliminate demand—it drives it underground. The same dynamic applies to CSAM:

  • Dark web markets for real CSAM remain robust because offenders cannot legally obtain AI alternatives.
  • Law enforcement resources are stretched thin trying to prosecute both real and AI CSAM, rather than focusing on the most severe cases.
  • Offenders who would otherwise use AI CSAM are forced into the black market, where they may encounter and contribute to real abuse material.

Legalizing AI CSAM would flood the market with a non-exploitative alternative, making real CSAM less accessible and less desirable.

3. The Psychological Reality: Demand Does Not Disappear

Some argue that legalizing AI CSAM would only encourage more people to engage in such material. However, this ignores basic economic and psychological principles:

  • Substitution effect: If a legal, risk-free alternative exists, many offenders will shift their consumption away from real CSAM.
  • Risk aversion: Currently, possessing any CSAM—real or AI—carries severe legal consequences. By decriminalizing AI material, we reduce the incentive for offenders to take risks by seeking out real abuse imagery.
  • Harm minimization: Just as needle exchange programs reduce HIV transmission among drug users without increasing drug use, legal AI CSAM would reduce real-world harm without necessarily increasing the overall prevalence of problematic behavior.
